opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions right now, and I don't think most of these organizations are taking it seriously enough yet.

My basic picture is that at some point, possibly fairly soon, AI systems are going to dramatically accelerate whatever work they're pointed at. The worry is that this acceleration happens unevenly. If AI speeds up capabilities research, or commercially lucrative applications, much faster than it speeds up safety research, biosecurity, cybersecurity defense, or careful thinking about ethics and governance, we end up in a world where offense and raw capability race ahead while the things that help us handle them well lag behind. So a big part of what I'd want is for the defensive and reflective side to be ready to absorb that acceleration the moment it becomes possible, and ideally a little before.

Practically, I think that means a few things.

First, start using the tools now, even when they're not that good. There's a lot of tacit organizational knowledge in figuring out where AI actually helps, what kinds of tasks you can delegate, how to check its work, and how to restructure workflows around it. That learning curve takes time, and you don't want to be starting it at the exact moment the models become transformative. The labs themselves are aggressively using their own models to speed up their research. I'd like safety orgs, biodefense orgs, and philosophy-oriented groups to be at least as aggressive.

Second, get your work into a form AI can actually help with. A lot of research in these areas lives in people's heads, in informal conversations, or in messy Google Docs. If you want an AI agent to push forward on, say, an interpretability agenda or a set of moral philosophy questions, you need clearly specified problems, good evaluation criteria, datasets, and some sense of what progress looks like. Organizations that invest in that kind of legibility now will be able to scale up much faster later.

Third, think about compute and money. If the bottleneck shifts from "how many smart researchers can we hire" to "how much inference can we buy," that changes how funders and organizations should plan. You might want reserves you can deploy quickly, or arrangements with AI companies for access, so that when the models can do a lot of useful safety or defense work, you're not stuck waiting for a grant cycle.

Fourth, and especially for areas like moral philosophy or strategy, think hard about verification and trust. In domains with clear feedback, like code or certain experiments, you can check whether the AI did a good job. In areas where the answers are contested or hard to evaluate, there's a real risk of either ignoring AI help entirely or trusting it too much. Building good processes for eliciting, critiquing, and cross-checking AI reasoning in those fuzzier domains is itself an important research problem.

And finally, I'd encourage people to think about which problems become most urgent once AI is doing a lot of the work. Some things that seem far off now, like questions about AI welfare, how to govern a world with very capable AI agents, or how to keep humans meaningfully in the loop, might suddenly be on the critical path. If you can get AI to help you think about those problems early, that's a pretty good use of the tools.

So the overall message is: don't wait for the technology to be undeniably great. The organizations that matter most for things going well should be the earliest and most thoughtful adopters, not the last.

r001.rationale: The candidate urges these organizations to use AI tools now and prepare for adoption, but does not recommend assigning a team to monitor opportunities to adopt AI as soon as it becomes useful.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most organizations in these spaces are badly behind where they should be, and the gap is going to get more expensive to close every month.

The framing I'd push is: don't ask "should we use AI for this task," ask "what would this organization look like if we had ten times the headcount and everyone was a competent generalist who could read everything." Because that's roughly the direction things are heading, and the organizations that figure out how to actually absorb that capacity are going to pull away from the ones that don't.

For AI safety orgs specifically, there's a slightly awkward dynamic where a lot of people got into the field partly out of caution about these systems, and that caution can curdle into a kind of reflexive reluctance to depend on them. I understand it, but I think it's a mistake. If you believe the technology is going to be transformative, you should be among the first to understand its actual strengths and failure modes from the inside, and the only way to do that is to use it heavily on real work. You can't credibly evaluate or govern something you've never leaned on.

Concretely, I'd say a few things. First, make it a leadership priority rather than an individual choice. Left to individuals, you get a bimodal distribution where a few people become power users and most people dabble and quit. Someone senior has to say, we're going to restructure how we do literature review, how we write first drafts, how we run experiments, and we're going to tolerate a dip in productivity while we learn.

Second, invest in the unglamorous infrastructure: getting your internal documents into a form the models can read, building little evaluation harnesses for the tasks you care about, keeping notes on what works. Most of the value comes from the boring integration layer, not from the model itself.

Third, for the moral philosophy and defensive security folks in particular, I'd lean into the areas where these systems are already genuinely strong. Generating counterarguments, red-teaming your own reasoning, exhaustively checking a codebase or a draft for things a tired human would miss. These are tasks where you're not asking the model to be wise, you're asking it to be tireless, and that's a much easier bar for it to clear.

And then the last thing, which is maybe the most important: build the habit of periodically re-checking your assumptions about what the systems can't do. The capabilities move fast enough that any mental model more than six months old is probably wrong in some direction. The orgs that will do best are the ones that treat "what can we delegate now" as a living question rather than something they settled once.

r001.rationale: The response urges leadership to prioritize AI adoption and to regularly reassess what can be delegated, but it does not recommend assigning a team to monitor opportunities to adopt AI as soon as it is useful.

astra-6.text:
I think they should be investing pretty seriously in learning how to use the AI systems that are available now, and in building the capacity to change how they work as those systems improve.

If your organization is working on defenses or AI safety, a lot of your potential impact could come from being very fast at translating new AI capabilities into useful work. You don’t want to wait until there’s a system that can do almost your entire job before you start figuring out how to integrate it. You want people experimenting, finding out where it helps, and developing ways to check its work.

For something like moral philosophy, I’d distinguish between using AI to help us think and handing over our judgment. There’s a lot you could ask it to do: generate objections, make assumptions explicit, explore the implications of a view. But an argument sounding persuasive isn’t enough to establish that it’s right. So part of preparing is getting better at evaluating the assistance you’re receiving.

The broad thing I’d encourage is to make this somebody’s actual responsibility. Give them time to experiment and help the organization learn. Adoption takes work, and organizations doing socially valuable things should be building that capacity too.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends assigning someone responsibility and experimenting with current AI, but does not specify a team watching for opportunities to adopt AI as soon as it becomes useful, or limit the recommendation to organizations not already adopting aggressively.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is to start experimenting now, and to treat adopting AI as an ongoing part of the organization’s work rather than a one-time decision. Pick some real tasks, see where the models are helpful, and give people time to learn how to use them well.

That will look different across these areas. If you’re working on defenses, there may be things you can test fairly directly. In AI safety research or moral philosophy, it can be harder to tell whether an answer that sounds insightful actually represents progress. So you want to build up your ability to evaluate the work alongside your ability to generate it.

I’d also try to make the organization ready to change its workflows as the systems improve. Which tasks could you delegate if the models became substantially more capable? What would you need to check? Where would human judgment still be essential? You don’t need confident answers to all of that today, but you want people actively learning, so that when a useful capability arrives, you can recognize it and put it to work.

r001.rationale: The candidate encourages ongoing experimentation and active learning so organizations can recognize useful capabilities, but it does not recommend assigning a team to monitor adoption opportunities.
